vignette:
The Weight of the Collapse

Marco is twenty-four years old, the kind of young man who grew up believing that if you work hard enough and pay close enough attention, you can catch the mistakes before they become disasters. It is a philosophy that served him well - first as a student, then as a QA engineer at a mid-sized software firm, where his job is essentially to find what is broken before anyone else does. He is methodical, detail-oriented, precise. He trusted those qualities once. He is less sure about them now.

Eighteen months ago, Marco was visiting his hometown in Colombia for his cousin's quinceañera. The celebration was held in a rented event hall on the edge of the city - a building that, as investigators would later confirm, had been constructed with substandard materials and falsified safety inspections. Midway through the evening, with nearly two hundred people inside, a section of the roof collapsed. Marco was near the back of the hall when it happened. He remembers the sound first - not a crash, exactly, but a low, structural groan that seemed to come from everywhere at once - and then the ceiling came down on the dance floor where, moments before, his younger cousin had been laughing.

He survived with a laceration on his forearm and bruised ribs. Eleven people did not survive. His cousin was not among the dead, but she spent three weeks in the hospital with a broken pelvis and a fractured wrist. Marco spent those three weeks at her bedside, translating for doctors, coordinating with family, and not sleeping. He told everyone he was fine. He flew back to the United States two weeks after she was discharged and returned to work the following Monday.

For a while, the busyness held things together. But within a few months, the seams began to show. Marco starts most mornings with a low, unspecific dread that he cannot name or locate. He lies awake cataloguing sounds - the building settling, a car alarm outside, the hum of his refrigerator - and his body responds to each one with the same flooding alertness it would reserve for genuine danger. When he does sleep, he returns to the hall. Sometimes in the dream he is still near the back. Sometimes he is on the dance floor.

At work, the hypervigilance that once made him an excellent QA engineer has turned against him. He reviews the same lines of code four and five times, certain he has missed something catastrophic. He has flagged three critical bugs in the past year that turned out to be non-issues, and each false alarm leaves him more shaken, not less. His manager has noticed that he seems distracted. Marco has not told him why.

He has stopped going to crowded places when he can avoid it. He skipped a friend's birthday at a restaurant last spring, claiming he was sick. He has not been inside a large public building - a mall, a concert venue, a stadium - since he came home. He tells himself this is reasonable. He knows, in a quieter part of himself, that it is not.

What troubles Marco most is something harder to articulate than fear. It is the feeling that the world is structurally unsound in a way it was not before - that the surfaces people walk on and the ceilings above their heads are held up by paperwork and wishful thinking, and that he alone understands this. He does not share this with people. He is not sure they would believe him, and he is not entirely sure they would be wrong not to.

He came to therapy because his mother asked him to. He sits in the chair across from his therapist with his arms folded loosely, answering questions carefully, the way he reviews code - looking for the right answer, still not entirely convinced he deserves to find it.
